transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-06 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood Product), Samir (Polaris CTO), Elena (Platform Eng), Marcus (SRE), Jin (Security)

---
Auto-generated summary (may be rough):
We walked through streaming failure modes when long history + high TPS collide. Highlighted how Console telemetry surfaces per-route token cost, streaming latency, and eviction of K V cache. Demonstrated Optimize suggestions for batching and quant profiles. Agreed to run a 1-hour bench and exchange prompts/security docs.

Topics covered: console dashboards, tracer/latency heatmaps, graceful fallback to lower-capacity model, session truncation, retry windows, KV cache eviction, prefix caching, telemetry alerts, cost run rate.

Action items (see metadata): Maya to send cost spreadsheet, Liam to run bench, Samir to provide prompts.

Transcript body:
00:00:04 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, is the timing OK on your side?
00:00:08 Samir Patel: Yeah this is good. We also have Elena and Marcus on to talk about runbook stuff, Jin is on the line for security questions.
00:00:21 Maya Chen: Awesome. Quick agenda: do a walkthrough of behavior under long-context + high TPS, show Console telemetry and an Optimize playbook, then agree next steps. Sound good?
00:00:29 Elena Ruiz: Yep, would love to see telemetry—our biggest pain is we only notice problems after customers complain.
00:01:12 Liam O'Connor: Right, so we'll start by reproducing a failure pattern we see a lot: concurrent sessions with >32k tokens of history, frequent user turns, and bursts hitting 200–500 TPS for short windows. That triggers queueing and sometimes streaming stalls.
00:01:45 Marcus Lee: When you say stalls, is that server-side backpressure or client disconnects? We've seen both.
00:01:53 Liam O'Connor: Mostly server-side queueing then the streaming chunk producer slows down. On our side the runtime will try batching but if KV cache thrashes it can increase per-token latency and you'll see chunk gaps.
00:02:17 Samir Patel: Can you show us where we would see that in Console?
00:02:25 Liam O'Connor: Yep. (screen share notes) On the per-route dashboard you'll see token throughput and also the streaming latency heatmap. When KV eviction's happening you'll see latency spikes correlated with a higher disk activity metric and a drop in cache hit rate.
00:03:08 Elena Ruiz: The dashboard term "KV cache" is it the same as our prior memcache? We have a memcached layer in front of our app.
00:03:15 Liam O'Connor: It's different—this is the model's KV cache; think of it like the model context key/value cache in the runtime. Apologies if the auto-transcript sometimes says K V as separate letters.
00:03:41 Jin Park: Security quick question: if cache evictions happen, is any PII written to persistent logs? We need to know for compliance.
00:03:50 Priya Nanda: Good callout. By default the runtime does not persist raw user content in logs. We emit telemetry aggregates and hashed prompt IDs; raw prompts can be optionally recorded only under a specific audit setting, and that would be controlled under Private deployments or per-customer retention flags.
00:04:23 Samir Patel: We run a mixture: some PHI-like notes and some generic customer queries. Data residency is important.
00:04:30 Maya Chen: Understood. We'll include retention/KMS notes in the follow-up packet.
00:05:01 Liam O'Connor: Back to failure modes—we demo two scenarios: first, streaming backpressure during a TPS spike while sessions keep growing; second, steady high TPS with long prefix history that forces repeated KV fills and thrashing.
00:05:26 Liam O'Connor: (demo) Here's a synthetic workload hitting 350 TPS for 8 minutes with session histories of 45k tokens. Notice the streaming timeline. See the step where several streams drop into a "chunk gap" state at 00:05:40?
00:05:49 Elena Ruiz: I can see the gap. Why do streams not retry immediately?
00:05:55 Liam O'Connor: We have a few layered protections: we try to fill the response buffer and stream partial chunks while the runtime recomputes KV pages. If the tail latency exceeds the streaming TTL, the client side may time out (and the socket closes). It depends on client timeout settings.
00:06:28 Marcus Lee: So is the recommended pattern to increase client-side timeouts? That feels like band-aid.
00:06:35 Maya Chen: Exactly, it's not ideal. The recommended playbook is multi-pronged: prefix caching, shorter effective history per request with reconstructive prompts, model quantization to reduce kernel runtime, and a routing fallback to a lower-capacity but compatible model for tail cases.
00:07:03 Samir Patel: Routing fallback — would that change output quality too much for us? We do a lot of clinical summarization, quality regression risks are a concern.
00:07:12 Priya Nanda: We showed earlier how Optimize can recommend a smaller model with a specific quant profile that has minimal quality delta on your prompts. Liam, can you pull up the Optimize eval?
00:07:21 Liam O'Connor: Sure. (switching) Here is an Optimize run we did with a similar medical note workload: we compared LLM-XL vs LLM-Lite quant8. The rouge/bertlike scores were within a few percent on our prompt set; latency per token dropped ~25% and cost per token dropped ~40%.
00:08:03 Elena Ruiz: That sounds promising. How do we validate for Polaris-specific prompts?
00:08:09 Liam O'Connor: Bring us a 100–200 prompt sample (anonymized) and we'll run the Optimize eval and return a delta matrix—plus we can run a human-in-the-loop QA pass.
00:08:33 Samir Patel: We can do that. Next, on the telemetry side, can we get alerting when KV hit rate drops below a threshold?
00:08:40 Priya Nanda: Yes, Console supports alert rules on any metric, including KV hit rate, per-route streaming latency p99, and token-cost burn rate. You can tie those to webhook integrations or PagerDuty.
00:09:06 Marcus Lee: On webhooks, can we include the session id and masked prompt id? We need to correlate with internal traces.
00:09:12 Liam O'Connor: Yep, we include a trace_id and masked prompt hash. Full plaintext prompts are never included unless you enable debug logging.
00:09:34 Jin Park: About Private deployment — our security team prefers on-prem because of FIPS KMS integration; do you have any guidance for streaming behavior differences on Private vs Hosted?
00:09:49 Priya Nanda: The runtime behaves the same; the main difference is you control network egress and the KMS. Performance differences usually come down to instance GPU types and NICs. We have a recommended instance profile for long-context workloads (A100-class with NVMe for swap/kvspill).
00:10:15 Elena Ruiz: Can you expand on KV spill? We've seen I/O spikes that map to spikes in streaming latency.
00:10:22 Liam O'Connor: KV spill is when the in-GPU KV can't hold the working set so it spills to host memory or NVMe. Spilling adds tens to hundreds of ms per token depending on bus and IO patterns. Optimize can surface the expected spill rate for a given session length distribution.
00:10:55 Samir Patel: Ok. Let's talk through a runbook: if we see streaming gaps, what is the immediate remediation?
00:11:03 Maya Chen: Quick triage: 1) check Console p99 streaming latency and KV hit rate; 2) if p99 > threshold, enable fallback routing to lite model for affected route; 3) temporarily raise client streaming TTL and mark affected sessions for async completion (post-process); 4) open a bench with Redwood to test prefix-trim settings.
00:11:28 Marcus Lee: How do we automate fallback routing?
00:11:33 Liam O'Connor: You can set routing policies in the deployment config: by latency SLO, cost SLO, or explicit error patterns. We can do a canary that routes 5% to the lite model and keep quality metrics tracked.
00:11:50 Elena Ruiz: Is there an A/B mechanism to compare output quality live?
00:11:53 Priya Nanda: Yes, Console supports side-by-side diffing of outputs for a sampled percentage. We surface quality deltas and allow you to set automatic thresholds for rollback.
00:12:20 Samir Patel: Great. During the demo I also noticed some mis-labeled speakers in the transcript earlier; any comment?
00:12:28 Maya Chen: The auto-transcription can sometimes misassign, especially with accents. The Fireflies export is independent. Noted.
00:12:45 Liam O'Connor: Back to the bench plan — we'll run two bench vectors: steady-state 200 TPS for 30 minutes with 20–30k token history, and spike test with 400 TPS bursts for 10 minutes with 40–50k history. We'll measure p50/p95/p99 streaming latency, percent of streams with chunk gaps, and cost/tokens.
00:13:20 Elena Ruiz: Can we add server-side metrics like NVMe IO and GPU memory pressure in the trace?
00:13:27 Liam O'Connor: Yes we'll include host-level metrics and correlate traces.
00:13:40 Samir Patel: What's an acceptable threshold for chunk gaps?
00:13:44 Priya Nanda: Typically we'd aim for <1% stream chunk gap under your SLO, and set alerting at 2%. But for long-context workloads you may accept higher if you have async fallbacks.
00:14:05 Marcus Lee: For the fallback model, what's the common quality loss we see in practice?
00:14:09 Liam O'Connor: It varies by prompt set; low-quality loss is typical with good quant profiles. In our internal tests we saw 3–6% relative quality loss on summaries for many enterprise prompt sets.
00:14:37 Samir Patel: OK. Can you also walk through cost controls? If we switch many users to fallback, cost changes.
00:14:45 Maya Chen: In Console you can set per-route cost caps and automatic routing when burn-rate exceeds X. Also Optimize recommends batching and quant settings to reduce per-token cost.
00:15:02 Elena Ruiz: Do you recommend client-side batching or server-side?
00:15:08 Liam O'Connor: Server-side continuous batching is powerful for small prompts, but if you can aggregate user turns server-side before calling the API you'll get additional savings. Optimize will quantify that benefit for your workload.
00:15:36 Samir Patel: Let's talk about timeouts—if the client has a 30s timeout and the server is in a spill-threshold, what's better: increase timeout or change application UX to an async completion?
00:15:49 Priya Nanda: UX async completion is best practice for long ops. Increase timeout only as a temporary measure. Also consider sending partial streaming chunks and client-side placeholders so users see partial text while we finish the rest.
00:16:10 Jin Park: For audit, if we switch to async post-process, how is data stored and is it encrypted?
00:16:16 Priya Nanda: Async artifacts are stored in the customer's configured storage; in Hosted we support customer-managed KMS for encrypting at rest. We'll include KMS notes in the follow up.
00:16:41 Samir Patel: Cool. Any other Gotchas?
00:16:46 Liam O'Connor: One we see often: client libraries that re-open streams aggressively on partial timeouts, creating thundering herd. We recommend jittered exponential backoff.
00:17:02 Marcus Lee: We had that exact issue last month. Do you have instrumentation to detect re-open loops?
00:17:08 Liam O'Connor: Yes Console shows connection churn metrics and you can alert on a high rate of new stream connections per session id.
00:17:29 Maya Chen: Alright, quick demo of Optimize suggestions now—this is a pre-run with an anonymized medical prompt set. Notice recommended quant profile Q4_128 and a batching window of 20ms for better latency/cost tradeoff.
00:17:55 Elena Ruiz: The Q4_128 sounds unfamiliar—what's the impact on memory?
00:18:01 Liam O'Connor: It reduces per-token memory and compute kernel costs. There's a small accuracy delta which Optimize quantifies.
00:18:18 Samir Patel: We'll want to run an offline validation.
00:18:22 Liam O'Connor: Totally. Bring the prompts and we'll run the Optimize suite.
00:18:40 Maya Chen: Ok next let's outline the pilot: 1) exchange prompts and retention requirements; 2) Redwood runs bench and Optimize run; 3) mutual review of quality deltas and rollback thresholds; 4) 2-week pilot at 5–10% traffic with side-by-side diffing and alerts.
00:19:10 Samir Patel: Pilot metrics: p99 streaming latency under 1.5s, chunk gap <1%, quality delta <5% on summaries, and cost per 1k tokens under target X.
00:19:29 Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll put that in the SOW.
00:19:36 (longer pause, troubleshooting audio)
00:22:10 Liam O'Connor: Quick note—we sometimes see the transcript generator mis-label speakers and AI microservices. Ignore typos like "redwood dedicate" in the transcript.
00:23:00 Elena Ruiz: Understood. Could you also add example fallback policy configs?
00:23:05 Priya Nanda: We'll add those to the shared folder: JSON snippets for routing policies, canary config, and alert rules.
00:24:10 Samir Patel: Anything else on security? Jin?
00:24:15 Jin Park: We'll want to review the SOC2 plus any side-channel mitigation notes for on-prem. Also KMS integration docs.
00:24:22 Maya Chen: We'll attach SOC2/ISO artifacts and KMS integration notes in the follow-up.
00:25:00 Marcus Lee: One operational ask—what's the recommended autoscale policy shape for spikes?
00:25:10 Liam O'Connor: Use a two-tier autoscale: fast reactive buffer for bursts (scale up quickly to absorb spikes) and a slower baseline scale for sustained traffic to avoid oscillation. We'll include example HPA-like configs.
00:25:36 Elena Ruiz: Do you support warm pools for models to reduce spin-up?
00:25:41 Priya Nanda: Yes dedicated pools can be reserved; you can keep a rumble of capacity warm for critical routes.
00:26:10 Samir Patel: Great, let's capture the concrete timeline. We plan to: send prompts by EOD 2026-04-09, bench run by Redwood 2026-04-10, and pilot kickoff 2026-04-15.
00:26:25 Maya Chen: We'll align on that and share calendar invites.
00:26:40 (wrap-up)
00:26:50 Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood to run bench and Optimize eval; share cost/latency spreadsheet and routing policy snippets; Polaris to share prompts, retention requirements, and acceptance criteria.
00:27:10 Samir Patel: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
00:27:15 Elena Ruiz: Thanks.
00:27:20 Jin Park: Thanks.
00:27:25 Maya Chen: We'll follow up with notes and the SOW.
